issues.title: Unilateral Trustee Rate Increases Without Cap
issues.description: Section 4.7(a) allows the Trustee to increase compensation rates annually with only 10 days' notice to holders, without requiring approval from the Bankruptcy Court or the Committee, and without any cap on the increase amount . This is problematic for the Debtor and the estate because the Trustee could significantly increase rates over time, depleting Trust Assets at the expense of creditors. The provision should require Committee approval or impose a reasonable cap.
issues.revision: ... Trustee may increase said compensation by no more than five percent (5%) per year upon ten (10) days'
issues.comment: We introduced a 5% annual cap on trustee compensation increases to protect estate assets and ensure creditor recoveries are not undermined by unconstrained fee escalation over the life of the Trust.

location.matched_text: Trustee may increase said compensation upon ten (10

judgment.reason: The provision clearly permits annual rate increases without a cap or further approval. The issue concerns commercial protection, not uncertainty in construing the text.

issues.title: Committee Can Remove Trustee Without Cause
issues.description: Section 5.2 allows the Committee to remove the Trustee "without cause" . While removal for Cause is appropriately defined, unlimited removal without cause gives the Committee disproportionate power and could destabilize the Trust's administration. From the Debtor's perspective, an abrupt removal could disrupt ongoing liquidation and litigation, harming the estate. Consider requiring at minimum reasonable written notice (e.g., 30 days) and a transition period before removal without cause takes effect.
issues.revision: ... by the Committee without cause upon not less than thirty (30) days' prior written notice to the Trustee and the Bankruptcy Court.
issues.comment: We revised this provision to require 30 days' prior written notice before a without-cause removal, ensuring orderly transition of Trust administration and preserving continuity of ongoing liquidation and litigation consistent with the estate's fiduciary obligations.

location.matched_text: by filing not less than ninety (90) days’ prior written notice of the proposed effective date of resignation with the Bankruptcy Court

judgment.reason: The Committee’s right to remove the Trustee without cause is unambiguous. The absence of notice or transition protections is a negotiation issue rather than a construction defect.

issues.title: Low Threshold for Committee Approval of Asset Dispositions
issues.description: Section 3.3(e) requires Committee approval only for the sale, liquidation, abandonment, or disposition of assets with a gross fair market value of $5,000 or more . This is an extremely low threshold that could create significant administrative burden, slowing down the Trust's liquidation process and potentially increasing costs. From the Debtor's perspective, a higher threshold (e.g., $25,000 or $50,000) would allow for more efficient administration while still providing meaningful Committee oversight over material transactions.
issues.revision: The Trustee shall sell, liquidate, abandon or otherwise dispose of an asset with a gross fair market value of $525,000 or more only pursuant ...
issues.comment: We increased the approval threshold to $25,000 to strike a more practical balance between Committee oversight and efficient trust administration, consistent with the scale of assets typically involved in liquidating trusts of this nature.

judgment.reason: The $5,000 approval threshold is definite and readily applicable. Whether it is administratively inefficient does not create ambiguity.

issues.title: Broad Exculpation Extends to All Trustee Agents
issues.description: Section 4.3(a) exculpates not only the Trustee but also all attorneys, accountants, professionals, employees, and "any other duly designated agent or representative" from liability for anything other than willful misconduct, gross negligence, or fraud . This is quite broad — excluding ordinary negligence as a standard of liability for all these parties means the Debtor's estate has very limited recourse if professionals retained by the Trustee act negligently. Consider narrowing the exculpation for non-Trustee parties to at least include ordinary negligence.

issues.comment: Blanket exculpation of all Trustee-designated agents and professionals from ordinary negligence liability is overbroad and disproportionately limits the estate's remedies; exculpation at this level should be reserved for the Trustee itself, not the full range of retained professionals.

issues.description: Section 4.8 provides that the Trustee shall serve without bond . Given that the Trustee will be handling potentially significant Trust Assets with broad authority and limited liability (only for willful misconduct, gross negligence, or fraud), the absence of a bond requirement removes a layer of financial protection for the Debtor and the beneficiaries. The Debtor should consider requiring a bond or at minimum requiring the Trustee to maintain appropriate insurance coverage.

issues.description: Section 8.1 allows any substantive provision of this Trust Agreement to be amended by the Trustee with Committee approval alone . The Debtor is entirely excluded from the amendment process, meaning the agreement could be materially modified without the Debtor's knowledge or consent. While the Plan controls over inconsistencies, amendments that don't directly conflict with the Plan but still affect the Debtor's interests could be made unilaterally. Consider requiring notice to, or consent of, the Debtor for material amendments.

issues.title: No Deadline for Distribution After Liquidation
issues.description: Section 3.6 states the Trustee shall make distributions "within a reasonable time after liquidation of all assets" , but does not define what constitutes a "reasonable time." This vague standard could allow distributions to be delayed indefinitely. From the Debtor's perspective (concerned with finality and winding down), a specific timeframe — such as 90 or 120 days — would provide more certainty and help ensure prompt closure.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Class 1 claims
judgments.reason: “Class 1 claims” is governed by the agreement’s express incorporation of Plan definitions. Repeating the definition locally would improve convenience but is not necessary to resolve meaning.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Chapter 11 Case
judgments.reason: The preamble identifies the pending Chapter 11 case by number and incorporates Plan definitions. In context, “Chapter 11 Case” has a sufficiently clear referent.

judgments.title: Mandatory Custodian Requirement May Be Overly Restrictive
judgments.reason: “The Trustee shall use a custodian” is mandatory and unambiguous. The expense or inconvenience of that requirement is a negotiation concern.

judgments.title: Successor Trustee Acceptance Lacks Release of Outgoing Trustee
judgments.reason: Section 5.3 does not release the outgoing Trustee, but the absence of a release is not ambiguous. The proposed release would add substantive liability protection.

judgments.title: Amendment Requires Only Trustee and Committee Approval
judgments.reason: Section 8.1 clearly permits amendment by the Trustee with Committee approval and does not require Debtor participation. The requested Debtor notice or consent is an additional protection, not a cure for ambiguity.

judgments.title: Notice Provision Limited to Regular Mail Only
judgments.reason: Section 9.6’s mail rule and Section 3.3(f)’s specific authorization of email for Committee procedures can be harmonized because they address different notice settings. There is no direct contradiction.

judgments.title: Notice Provision Limited to Mail Only
judgments.reason: The general mail provision and the specific email procedures for Committee meetings and approvals can be read together without contradiction. Expanding permissible delivery methods is a modernization proposal rather than a construction cure.
